name: Weeb Ewbank
tagline: A teacher behind the Jets’ greatest breakthrough
intro: Ewbank was a teacher who understood how to reach his players. After the painful Heidi Game loss, he had the team choose its own curfew penalty, turning discipline into a shared responsibility. His work with Joe Namath helped the Jets become AFL champions and then Super Bowl III winners. He had already won NFL championships with Baltimore, giving him a unique place in both leagues.
why: He helped a young franchise turn belief into a championship team. His patient work with players connected the running game, passing game and defense.

moments.title: A name from childhood
moments.text: His younger brother’s pronunciation of Wilbur became the nickname football would remember.

moments.title: One more year upstairs
moments.text: Ewbank retired from coaching after 1973 and remained the Jets’ general manager for the 1974 season.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced black-and-white portrait of Jets coach Weeb Ewbank

name: Winston Hill
tagline: The protector who kept showing up
intro: Hill gave the Jets something every quarterback needs: a protector they could trust for years. Released by Baltimore, he found his football home in New York and became a fixture on the line, including the Super Bowl III championship team. His 195 consecutive games and eight combined AFL All-Star and NFL Pro Bowl selections tell the story of that dependability, rather than a single celebrated play.
why: A reliable tackle gives everyone around him room to work. Hill’s long service helped hold the Jets’ line together through their championship years.

moments.title: On both sides of the line
moments.text: His eight all-star selections included five at left tackle and three at right tackle.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced portrait of Winston Hill in his white Jets No.75 uniform

name: Joe Klecko
role: Defensive end, tackle and nose tackle
tagline: Boxing strength and three positions on the line
intro: Klecko brought a boxer’s competitive edge to the defensive line. At Temple he compiled a 25–2 boxing record and even sparred with Joe Frazier. In New York, that strength and technical skill made him central to the Sack Exchange. His versatility mattered as much as his power: he earned Pro Bowl recognition at defensive end, defensive tackle and nose tackle before finally entering Canton in 2023.
why: Moving between end, tackle and nose let him solve different problems for the defense. That versatility gave the Sack Exchange much of its shape.

moments.title: Before sacks became official
moments.text: The Hall credits Klecko with 20.5 sacks in 1981, before sacks became an official NFL statistic in 1982.

moments.title: Back for the playoffs
moments.text: A ruptured knee tendon interrupted his 1982 season, but he returned for the Jets’ run to the AFC Championship Game.

name: Curtis Martin
tagline: Quiet work with a purpose beyond football
intro: Martin explained that football was not originally his deepest passion; it became a way to help other people. That purpose supported the patient, consistent work Jets fans saw every Sunday. He arrived in 1998, helped the team reach the AFC Championship Game, and won the NFL rushing title at 31 in 2004. His teammates’ regard lives on in the team MVP award bearing his name.
why: His consistency gave the offense a dependable starting point. His reasons for playing also connect the rushing records to the people he wanted to help.

moments.title: Seven straight in New York
moments.text: Martin rushed for at least 1,000 yards in each of his first seven Jets seasons.

name: Don Maynard
tagline: An original Titan who made every catch count
intro: Maynard helped turn a struggling new franchise into a champion. He was the first player to sign with the Titans, then became Joe Namath’s longtime receiving partner. His six catches and two touchdowns against Oakland sent the Jets to Super Bowl III. Away from the headlines, he was inventive about his craft, using custom soccer-style cleats to make sharp cuts and keep his legs fresh.
why: His partnership with Namath gave a young franchise a dangerous passing game. Their connection helped turn years of losing into a championship opportunity.

moments.title: The career ledger
moments.text: He retired with pro records of 633 catches and 11,834 receiving yards across his NFL and AFL career.

name: Joe Namath
tagline: The quarterback who made the guarantee stand
intro: Namath gave the young Jets a star and a belief they could beat anybody. His Super Bowl III victory remains the defining image, but the football thinking mattered too: when Baltimore’s coverage opened the running game, he kept using it. He had already become pro football’s first 4,000-yard passer in 1967. Discussing the Ring of Honor, he emphasized the teammates whose names would share it.
why: His confidence helped put the young league on equal terms with its older rival. On the field, reading the defense made that confidence useful.

moments.title: Two leagues wanted him
moments.text: The NFL’s Cardinals also drafted Namath. His reported $400,000 Jets contract in 1965 was a major signing for the AFL.

name: Larry Grantham
tagline: Leadership that lasted well beyond the huddle
intro: Grantham linked the original Titans to the Super Bowl champions. Undersized for a linebacker, he relied on speed, tackling and an understanding of the defense that teammates trusted. His care for teammates continued after football: he worked with Freedom House and helped arrange a proper funeral for former Jet Sam Walton after Walton died homeless. The story of No. 60 includes both leadership and loyalty.
why: His teammates trusted the way he understood the defense. His later care for former players made that sense of responsibility last beyond football.

moments.title: Chosen by his teammates
moments.text: The Jets voted Grantham their team MVP in 1971, near the end of his thirteen-season career.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced black-and-white portrait of Larry Grantham in Jets No.60

name: Freeman McNeil
tagline: Patient cuts and credit for the blockers
intro: McNeil was the rushing standard before Curtis Martin. He led the NFL in the shortened 1982 season, then ran for 202 yards and threw a touchdown pass in the playoff win at Cincinnati. When recalling that performance, he put the credit on the holes his linemen created. He left New York as its career rushing leader after spending every one of his 12 NFL seasons with the Jets.
why: His running helped carry the Jets into the playoffs. The way he remembered those games also kept the work of his blockers and teammates in view.

moments.title: The mark Martin would chase
moments.text: McNeil finished with 8,074 rushing yards and 1,798 carries, both Jets career records at his retirement.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Freeman McNeil carrying the football in his Jets No.24 uniform.

name: Gerry Philbin
tagline: A relentless motor on the championship defense
intro: Philbin’s calling card was the effort that never seemed to stop. He was small for a defensive end, yet teammates remembered his penetration against the run as clearly as his pass rush. He also helped connect the Jets to Buddy Ryan, recommending the coach he knew from Buffalo. His place on the AFL’s all-time first team reflects the defensive work behind the Super Bowl III breakthrough.
why: His pressure and run defense helped give the championship team its balance. The story also shows how long-standing relationships can help a defense grow together.

moments.title: Two years at the top
moments.text: Philbin earned AFL All-Star and All-Pro recognition after both the 1968 and 1969 seasons.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Gerry Philbin in Jets No.81 leaping to obstruct a pass

name: Al Toon
tagline: Consistency that teammates kept voting to honor
intro: Toon wanted consistency more than dramatic highs and lows. After his first six NFL games, he caught a pass in every remaining game of his career, a streak of 101. Teammates voted him their MVP three years running. Repeated concussions ended his playing career in 1992, but his eight seasons left a lasting standard for reliability at receiver and a strong connection with Jets fans.
why: A receiver who keeps showing up gives a quarterback someone to trust. Toon brought that reliability to an offense full of strong personalities.

moments.title: Six seasons leading the room
moments.text: Toon led the Jets in receptions in every season from 1986 through 1991.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Al Toon carrying the football in his Jets No.88 uniform.

name: Mark Gastineau
tagline: Speed, sacks and a very public celebration
intro: Gastineau made the pass rush impossible to ignore, with speed, sacks and the dance fans still asked him to recreate years later. He was part of the four-man Sack Exchange and set a then-NFL record with 22 sacks in 1984. Looking back before his Ring induction, he spoke about his faith and changed life, adding a personal chapter to the familiar football highlights.
why: His rush made the Jets’ defensive line a spectacle as well as a threat. His later reflections add a human voice to those familiar highlights.

moments.title: Five straight all-star seasons
moments.text: Gastineau earned five consecutive Pro Bowl selections beginning with the 1981 season.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Mark Gastineau tackling Bernie Kosar in his Jets No.99 uniform, in black and white.

name: Wesley Walker
tagline: A deep threat who kept finding new purpose
intro: Walker became a deep threat despite being legally blind in one eye and overcoming a serious college knee injury. He led the league in yards per catch as a rookie and spent his whole NFL career with the Jets. After football, he found another source of pride teaching physical education and coaching children. He said his experience with blindness also helped him encourage people facing their own difficulties.
why: His speed stretched the field for the Jets. His life after football shows how experience with an obstacle can become encouragement for someone else.

moments.title: A second-season breakthrough
moments.text: In 1978, Walker led the NFL with 1,169 receiving yards and averaged 24.4 yards per catch.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Wesley Walker running in his Jets No.85 uniform, in black and white.

name: Marty Lyons
tagline: From the Sack Exchange to granting wishes
intro: Lyons helped make the Sack Exchange, then kept finding ways to serve people beyond the line of scrimmage. He founded the Marty Lyons Foundation in 1982 to grant wishes to children with serious illnesses and received the NFL’s community-service honor in 1984. Jets fans later knew his voice from the radio booth, where he spent 22 seasons before moving into an ambassador role in 2024.
why: He connected three kinds of service: playing for teammates, telling the team’s story on radio and helping children through his foundation.

moments.title: Service became a team tradition
moments.text: Since 1990, the Jets have given the Marty Lyons Award to a player for his community work.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Marty Lyons in his Jets No.93 uniform rushing past a Cleveland blocker.

name: Wayne Chrebet
tagline: An overlooked receiver who earned his place
intro: Chrebet began at the back of a ten-man receiver depth chart after arriving undrafted from Hofstra. He finished with 580 regular-season catches and a place in Jets history. The path made him an easy player to identify with: an overlooked newcomer who kept earning his place. His Ring announcement surprised him in the stands, surrounded by the family and fans who had followed that journey.
why: His rise gave fans a familiar kind of hope: a chance earned through work. The relationships around that journey remained part of his Jets story.

moments.title: A handshake after defeat
moments.text: Chrebet remembered Leon Hess thanking every player individually when the team’s plane returned from its 1998 AFC Championship Game loss.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Wayne Chrebet seen from behind raising the football in his Jets No.80 uniform.

name: Leon Hess
tagline: An owner remembered through his everyday encounters
intro: Hess joined the five-man group that bought the financially troubled Titans in 1963, helping preserve the franchise that became the Jets. Players remembered the personal encounters as well as the business decisions. John Nitti recalled Hess valuing his offer to return salary while injured, even though union rules required payment. His ownership spanned the championship team and generations of Jets players.
why: His ownership links the franchise’s survival to its championship years. Players’ recollections also reveal how they experienced the man behind those decisions.

moments.title: The end of a long season
moments.text: Wayne Chrebet recalled Hess standing by the plane and thanking players individually after the 1998 AFC Championship Game loss.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Leon Hess in a black-and-white formal portrait.

name: Emerson Boozer
tagline: The block behind the championship touchdown
intro: Boozer’s best-known championship contribution was helping somebody else score. His block helped clear Matt Snell’s path on the Jets’ only touchdown in Super Bowl III. When the two entered the Ring together, their rings carried the name of that play, 19 Straight. He was also a productive runner in his own right, leading the AFL in rushing touchdowns in an injury-shortened 1967 season.
why: His work beside Snell shows how a decisive play depends on the teammate clearing its path. The backfield’s shared honor preserved that connection.

moments.title: A winning homecoming
moments.text: The Jets beat Miami 38–20 on the November 2015 day when Boozer and Snell entered the Ring together.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Emerson Boozer carrying the football in his Jets No.32 uniform, in black and white.

name: Matt Snell
tagline: The runner who gave the promise its force
intro: Snell gave the Jets’ biggest promise its physical foundation. He carried 30 times for 121 yards and their lone touchdown in Super Bowl III, while also catching passes and protecting Joe Namath. He had been the first member of his family to attend college before joining New York out of Ohio State. The Jets remembered that toughness and selflessness when he died in March 2026.
why: His running made the Super Bowl game plan work. Catching and blocking gave the Jets more ways to keep the offense moving around Namath.

moments.title: Useful through the air, too
moments.text: Four catches for forty yards took his Super Bowl III total to 161 yards from scrimmage.

moments.title: Another green prize
moments.text: The Jets’ retrospective recalls Sonny Werblin buying Snell a green car after Namath received the Super Bowl MVP prize.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Matt Snell, right in No.41, taking Joe Namath’s handoff in Super Bowl III

name: Kevin Mawae
tagline: The center who studied the names above him
intro: Mawae used to arrive at stadiums hours before kickoff, sit in the stands and read the names of great players. He wanted to be a good football player, not necessarily one of those names. His eight Jets seasons helped make that possible: he anchored the line for Curtis Martin and earned six Pro Bowl selections in New York. Entering the Ring put him alongside the teammates he treasured.
why: A center’s work helps the whole offense function. Mawae’s story connects that responsibility to the pride of earning a place among the team’s honored players.

moments.title: Every appearance was a start
moments.text: Mawae started all 118 regular-season games he played for the Jets. All seven of his NFL playoff appearances also came with New York.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Kevin Mawae raising his fist at the lectern with his Hall of Fame bust alongside.

name: D'Brickashaw Ferguson
tagline: A dependable protector, then a different calling
intro: Ferguson gave the Jets a decade of certainty at left tackle, starting every regular-season game from 2006 through 2015. His story continued after the helmet came off. Inspired by his mother and grandmother, both nurses, he completed a nursing degree at Jefferson in May 2025 and took a hospital job in New Jersey. The work changed, but his next chapter still centered on serving and protecting people.
why: His football career offered teammates years of reliability. His move into nursing carries the same concern for other people into a new kind of work.

moments.title: The postseason counted, too
moments.text: Alongside his 160 regular-season starts, Ferguson started seven playoff games for the Jets.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of D'Brickashaw Ferguson in his Jets No.60 uniform in a blocking stance.

name: Nick Mangold
tagline: An anchor whose friendships outlived the game
intro: Mangold became the center of the Jets’ line from his first season and spent his entire career with one club. Alongside D’Brickashaw Ferguson, he helped give playoff teams a dependable foundation. Tributes recalled his humor and the way he made people feel included as clearly as his toughness. After his death in October 2025, those friendships were an essential part of the way the Jets remembered him.
why: His work at center helped hold the offense together. The friendships teammates described give those playoff-era Jets a lasting human connection.

moments.title: A place among the franchise’s best
moments.text: Mangold made 171 starts, including seven in the postseason, and earned seven Pro Bowl selections.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Nick Mangold calling line assignments in his Jets No.74 uniform.

name: Darrelle Revis
tagline: Preparation that put an island on the field
intro: Revis Island was built through preparation, not just talent. Before his Ring induction, Revis recalled the hill runs and extra work behind his dream, and how coaches sometimes had to send him home from practice. That study let the Jets trust him one-on-one against leading receivers. His two spells in New York connected dominant coverage to a personal standard of arriving ready for every Sunday.
why: Trusting one cornerback against a leading receiver gives the defense more choices elsewhere. His preparation helped make that trust possible.

moments.title: The 2009 evidence
moments.text: Revis recorded six interceptions and 31 passes defended as the Jets led the league in pass defense.

moments.title: A full field against Miami
moments.text: His 2011 interception return against the Dolphins covered 100 yards.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Darrelle Revis and his mother Diana Askew unveiling his Hall of Fame bust.

name: Steve Atwater
tagline: A champion’s final season came in New York
intro: Atwater’s Jets story came at the end of an eleven-year NFL career. After ten seasons and two Super Bowl victories with Denver, the safety spent 1999 in New York, appearing in twelve games. That short stay connects the Jets to a celebrated defensive career, while leaving the championship years clearly rooted in Denver.
why: His profile gives the 1999 secondary its proper context: a veteran champion bringing a decade of experience into one final NFL season.

moments.title: An established reputation
moments.text: Atwater’s career included eight Pro Bowl selections and a place on the NFL’s 1990s All-Decade Team.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Steve Atwater speaking at a Hall of Fame ceremony in his gold jacket.

name: Alan Faneca
tagline: Veteran strength and a voice for others
intro: Faneca arrived in 2008 with a decade of experience from Pittsburgh. The left guard played all 32 regular-season games during his two years with the Jets, helping a line that carried the 2009 team into the AFC Championship Game. New York was a short but substantial chapter between his Steelers years and his final season in Arizona.
why: He brought experience to a young offensive line. His work with children also made a successful football career a source of practical encouragement.

moments.title: Meeting the children at camp
moments.text: During Jets camp in 2008, Faneca met youngsters from the Epilepsy Foundation of Long Island. He had been diagnosed at fifteen.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Alan Faneca in his gold Hall of Fame jacket beside his bronze bust.

name: Brett Favre
tagline: A short Jets stay with one explosive afternoon
intro: Favre joined the Jets during training camp in 2008 after a long career in Green Bay. He played all sixteen games that season, throwing for 3,472 yards and 22 touchdowns. After catching three scores against Arizona, Laveranues Coles described his excitement at playing alongside a legend and the chance to learn from him. Favre’s Jets career lasted a single season.
why: His brief visit produced a performance tied to Joe Namath’s franchise record, while Coles’s response captured what sharing the field with him meant.

moments.title: Six scores against Arizona
moments.text: On September 28, 2008, Favre threw six touchdown passes in a 56–35 win, matching Joe Namath’s Jets record.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Brett Favre in his gold Hall of Fame jacket beside his bronze bust.

name: Ty Law
tagline: A familiar rival brought his best interception season
intro: Law had spent ten seasons facing the Jets as a Patriot before joining New York in 2005. His first Jets season brought a career-high ten interceptions, enough to lead the NFL. After two seasons in Kansas City, he returned for seven games in 2008. Those two separate visits form his Jets story within a longer career across four teams.
why: His first Jets season turned a longtime divisional opponent into a leading playmaker. The later return gives his New York story two distinct chapters.

moments.title: A full season after injury
moments.text: A foot injury had cut short his 2004 season in New England. He played all sixteen Jets games the following year.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Ty Law in his gold Hall of Fame jacket beside his bronze bust.

name: Ronnie Lott
tagline: A legendary defender’s final chapter in New York
intro: Lott spent the final two seasons of his playing career with the Jets, appearing in 31 games in 1993 and 1994. The hard-hitting defensive back had already won four Super Bowls with San Francisco. In New York, he passed 1,000 career tackles and made his final three interceptions, all during the 1993 season. His Canton recognition covers that whole career.
why: His final seasons connect the Jets to an accomplished defensive career. They also give the 1993 and 1994 teams a veteran presence worth remembering.

moments.title: Experience across the secondary
moments.text: Lott earned Pro Bowl selections at cornerback, free safety and strong safety during his career.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Ronnie Lott standing beside his Hall of Fame bust against a stone wall.

name: Art Monk
tagline: A New York homecoming and another receiving record
intro: For Monk, joining the Jets in 1994 was also a return to New York. The White Plains native had built most of his career in Washington before arriving for one season in green. He caught 46 passes and three touchdowns, then broke Steve Largent’s consecutive-games reception record. Largent came to the Meadowlands to see the moment himself.
why: His Jets season joined a local homecoming to an important receiving milestone. Younger teammates also had the chance to learn directly from an established professional.

moments.title: His biggest Jets afternoon
moments.text: Monk caught five passes for 108 yards against Miami in November 1994, including a 69-yard reception.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Art Monk in his gold Hall of Fame jacket beside his bronze bust.

name: Bill Parcells
tagline: A turnaround on the sideline and beyond
intro: Parcells took over a Jets team coming off a 1–15 season. His first year, 1997, ended at 9–7; the next brought a 12–4 record, a division title and an AFC Championship Game appearance. He coached through 1999 before moving into full-time football operations for 2000. His Jets story includes both the sideline turnaround and the roster decisions that followed.
why: His arrival changed what the Jets could expect from a season. His later front-office role also connects the turnaround to the players who followed.

moments.title: Four picks in the first round
moments.text: After moving to football operations in 2000, Parcells helped assemble a draft that brought Shaun Ellis, John Abraham, Chad Pennington and Anthony Becht.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Bill Parcells in his green Jets coaching jacket

name: Ed Reed
tagline: A reunion late in a remarkable defensive career
intro: Reed arrived in November 2013 after an earlier stop in Houston that season. Signing with the Jets reunited the safety with Rex Ryan, a familiar coach from Baltimore. Reed played seven games for New York and collected three interceptions before his playing career ended. His brief Jets chapter came after eleven Ravens seasons and their Super Bowl victory.
why: His arrival brought a familiar relationship with Rex Ryan into the Jets’ secondary. The short stay produced a final group of interceptions in New York.

moments.title: A first Jets interception
moments.text: On December 8, 2013, Reed intercepted Oakland’s Matt McGloin on a pass intended for Andre Holmes.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Ed Reed in Jets No.22 returning the ball between Raiders defenders

name: John Riggins
tagline: The first thousand yards came as a Jet
intro: Riggins began his NFL career with the Jets, who selected him sixth overall in 1971. He spent five seasons in New York and reached 1,005 rushing yards in 1975, the first thousand-yard season of his career. Washington came next, along with the postseason performances that made him famous. The foundation of that powerful running style was already visible as a Jet.
why: His New York years show the beginning of the powerful runner remembered for Washington. The Jets were where he first crossed the thousand-yard mark.

moments.title: A rookie who caught passes, too
moments.text: Alongside 769 rushing yards in 1971, Riggins caught 36 passes for 231 yards.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced black-and-white photograph of John Riggins waving at his 1992 Hall of Fame induction.

name: Jason Taylor
tagline: A longtime opponent joined the playoff chase
intro: Taylor came to the Jets in 2010 after years of facing them with Miami. He played all sixteen regular-season games, recorded five sacks and joined the team’s run to the AFC Championship Game. The following season he returned to the Dolphins. His single year in New York sits inside a career whose greatest share was played across the division.
why: His one season shows how a familiar rival can become a useful teammate. He contributed to a Jets team playing deep into January.

moments.title: Two important points in Pittsburgh
moments.text: Taylor tackled Mewelde Moore in the end zone late in the Jets’ 22–17 win at Pittsburgh in December 2010.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Jason Taylor in his white Jets No.99 uniform

name: LaDainian Tomlinson
tagline: A new backfield and another chance in January
intro: Tomlinson spent his last two NFL seasons with the Jets after nine years in San Diego. In 2010, he rushed for 914 yards and caught 52 passes while sharing backfield work with Shonn Greene. He accepted a different workload in New York and continued to contribute as both a runner and receiver. The Jets’ January games gave that partnership its biggest stage.
why: His willingness to share the backfield helped the Jets manage a long season. A rested veteran then gave them two crucial postseason scores.

moments.title: Rest that paid off
moments.text: After sitting out the regular-season finale, Tomlinson ran for 82 yards and both Jets touchdowns in their 17–16 playoff win at Indianapolis.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of LaDainian Tomlinson in Jets No.21 running with the football

name: Ron Wolf
tagline: The talent evaluator behind a famous near miss
intro: Wolf’s Jets connection was in the personnel department. He worked as director of player personnel in 1990 and 1991 before becoming Green Bay’s general manager that November. His years finding players had begun with the Raiders in 1963. Canton honored him as a contributor, placing a talent evaluator alongside the players and coaches whose teams he helped build.
why: His story belongs alongside the people who found and developed players. A near miss in New York would later help shape football in Green Bay.

moments.title: One pick away from Favre
moments.text: Wolf rated Brett Favre the best prospect in the 1991 draft. Atlanta chose him one slot before the Jets could.

photo.alt: AI-enhanced photograph of Ron Wolf speaking at a microphone

Ron Wolf remembers the Favre draft

name: Dennis Byrd
tagline: An enduring example of recovery and family
intro: Dennis Byrd spent four seasons on the Jets’ defensive line before a neck injury in 1992 ended his playing career. His recovery and return to walking became part of the team’s identity. The Jets named their inspiration award after him and retired No. 90 in 2012. Byrd died in an Oklahoma car crash on October 15, 2016, at age fifty.
why: His place in Jets history rests in the relationships he built and the encouragement he gave teammates long after his playing career.

moments.title: A productive beginning
moments.text: Byrd recorded 27 sacks in 57 Jets games between 1989 and 1992.

moments.title: Why he chose ninety
moments.text: His older brother Dan had worn No. 90 in high school. Byrd chose the same number with the Jets to honor him.
